title: Kong Rong Gives Up the Larger Pears
text:
Kong Rong, who lived in the late Han dynasty and was a descendant of Confucius, was one of several brothers. When he was four years old, the family was given a plate of pears.

The boys were allowed to choose. Kong Rong did not grab for the biggest one, as small children usually do. He reached for the smallest pear on the plate.

The adults asked why he had chosen it. He answered that he was a small boy, so he ought to take the small one. Older brothers should have the larger pears.

The story was told about him throughout his family and later throughout China. Kong Rong grew up to be a well known scholar and official, but he is remembered above all for this one small act. Many centuries later the episode was placed in the Three Character Classic, the rhyming primer from which generations of Chinese children learned to read: "Rong at four could yield the pears."
lesson: Children learn generosity in small daily choices like who gets the bigger share. Notice and praise the moment a child chooses to give way.
source: Hou Hanshu, biography of Kong Rong, with commentary citing the Rong Biezhuan; Three Character Classic
caveat: The anecdote comes from a commentary rather than the main historical record and is a traditional story.
